title: From Ar-Ra'd to Al-Isra
intro: 24 days through five surahs, from Ar-Ra'd (The Thunder) to Al-Isra (The Night Journey).

posts.display: Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts.
posts.display_original: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ
posts.caption: Five surahs, 13 to 17, starting with Ar-Ra'd, "The Thunder" (43 verses). The standard Cairo edition marks it Medinan, though many scholars consider it Meccan. This famous line, part of a longer verse, ties a people's condition to what is within them. Classical commentators read it mainly as a warning that a people's blessings are not taken away until they change themselves; many Muslims today also quote it as a call to change for the better.

The verse that gives the surah its name. In the Quran all creation praises Allah in its own way, and here even the thunder glorifies Him, with the angels in awe. The point lies in the contrast: nature praises its Creator while some people still dispute about Him. A short prayer echoing this verse, reported from the Companion Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, is still said by many Muslims when they hear thunder.

posts.display: Such as persevere in seeking their Lord's Countenance and are regular in prayer and spend of that which We bestow upon them secretly and openly, and overcome evil with good. Theirs will be the sequel of the (heavenly) Home.
posts.caption: Part of a portrait of "men of understanding": patient in seeking their Lord's "Countenance" (wajh), regular in prayer, giving in private and in public. "Overcome evil with good" can also be read "repel evil with good", answering harm with kindness. "The sequel of the Home" means a good final end.

One of the most quoted verses in the Quran, and its point is simple: hearts find rest in remembering Allah. The verse first describes believers whose hearts are at peace, then states it as a general truth. Remembrance, dhikr, includes prayer, reading the Quran and repeating short phrases such as SubhanAllah (glory be to Allah) and Alhamdulillah (praise be to Allah).

Surah Ibrahim, the fourteenth, is Meccan with 52 verses, named after the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), whose prayer for Mecca comes near its end. This verse explains why every messenger spoke his own people's language: so the message would be clear to them. The Quran calls itself "a Lecture in Arabic" for the same reason (12:2).

The Prophet Musa (Moses) reminds his people of Allah's promise: gratitude, shukr, brings increase, and ingratitude has consequences. "Proclaimed" marks a solemn announcement. It is one of the best-known verses on gratitude, often quoted when Muslims speak of counting their blessings.

posts.display: Seest thou not how Allah coineth a similitude: A goodly saying, as a goodly tree, its root set firm, its branches reaching into heaven.
posts.caption: A famous parable: a good word is like a good tree, deep-rooted and reaching to the sky, and the next verse adds that it gives fruit in every season. Many early commentators took the "goodly saying" to be the declaration of faith, "There is no god but Allah", and the tree to be the date palm.

After listing gifts, from rain and fruit to ships, rivers, the sun, the moon, night and day, the surah concludes that Allah's favours are beyond counting. It then names the human failing it warns against: ingratitude. A near-identical line in An-Nahl (16:18) ends instead with Allah's forgiveness and mercy.

Al-Hijr, the fifteenth surah, is Meccan with 99 verses. Here, answering opponents who mocked the revelation, Allah declares that He sent down "the Reminder" (adh-dhikr), a name for the Quran, and that He Himself will guard it. Muslims understand this as Allah's promise to preserve the Quran. The surah is named after the rocky home of the people of Thamud (verse 80), traditionally linked with Hegra in north-west Arabia.

Two truths are set side by side: Allah is forgiving and merciful, and His punishment is real. Commentators often note that forgiveness and mercy are named first, before the warning. The verses are addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; "slaves" here translates 'ibad, Allah's servants, and "dolorous" is an old word for painful. They lead into the story of the guests of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham).

After recalling peoples destroyed for rejecting their messengers, Al-Hijr turns to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Creation has a purpose and the Hour, the Day of Judgment, is coming, so he is told to forgive. "Gracious forgiveness" renders as-safh al-jamil, a beautiful pardon; commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain it as overlooking the insults of his opponents in Mecca.

The closing verses of Al-Hijr speak to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while mockery in Mecca weighed on him. The answer offered is worship: praise, prostration and steady service. "The Inevitable" renders al-yaqin, literally "the certainty", which commentators explain as death.

posts.display: And thy Lord inspired the bee, saying: Choose thou habitations in the hills and in the trees and in that which they thatch.
posts.caption: An-Nahl, "The Bee", is the sixteenth surah: largely Meccan, with 128 verses, and so full of Allah's gifts that it is sometimes called the surah of blessings. Here the bee itself is a sign: its instinct to build and gather is presented as guidance from Allah. It is "inspired" (awha), the same verb the Quran uses for revelation to prophets. The next verse speaks of honey, with healing for people.

Every person begins knowing nothing. The verse lists what Allah gives instead: hearing, sight and hearts, af'ida, which in the Quran means the seat of understanding as well as feeling. The purpose named at the end is gratitude, a thread that runs through this whole surah.

In a few words this verse sums up the Quran's ethics: justice ('adl), kindness and excellence (ihsan), and giving to relatives, against shamelessness, wrongdoing and oppression. Many mosques close the Friday sermon with it, a custom often traced to the caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz in the early 700s. The Companion Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have called it the most comprehensive verse in the Quran for good and evil.

The promise is made to men and women alike, in the same words. "Quicken" means bring to life. Early commentators explained the "good life" (hayat tayyiba) in several ways, including contentment, lawful provision and happiness, and the reward is measured by the best of what a person did.

Addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, this verse became a guide for da'wah, inviting others to the faith: with wisdom (hikmah), good counsel and, where there is disagreement, discussion "in the better way". It leaves the final judgment of who is rightly guided to Allah.

Al-Isra, the seventeenth surah, is Meccan with 111 verses, named after the Night Journey in its first verse and also called Bani Isra'il (The Children of Israel). Here kindness to parents stands beside the worship of Allah. "Fie" renders uff, a sigh of irritation, and the verse rules out even that toward aging parents.

The passage on parents continues. "The wing of submission" is the image of a bird lowering its wing over its young, now turned in tenderness toward one's parents. The prayer at the end, Rabbi irhamhuma, is one of the most widely used Quranic prayers for parents, living or departed.

Everything in creation glorifies Allah, the verse says, though people do not understand how. This glorifying is tasbih, from the same root as SubhanAllah, "glory be to Allah". The verse ends on mercy: "Clement" renders Halim, the Forbearing, who does not rush to punish.

A foundational verse on human dignity: Allah has honoured the "Children of Adam", meaning all humanity. It names gifts given to every person, from travel by land and sea to good provision. Muslim writers often cite it when speaking of the dignity owed to every human being.

The point is confidence that truth outlasts falsehood: when truth comes, falsehood is bound to vanish. According to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited this verse when he entered Mecca in 630 CE, striking down the idols around the Kaaba. "Vanished away" renders zahaqa, to perish or pass away. Just before it comes a prayer for a sound entrance and a sound exit.

Commentators report that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was asked about the spirit, ar-ruh, as a test. The answer: it belongs to Allah's command, and human knowledge is only a little. Many commentators take "the Spirit" here to mean the soul that gives life. "Vouchsafed" is an old word for given.

Whether people call on Allah or on the Beneficent, Ar-Rahman, His are the most beautiful names. A report from Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari links the second half to Mecca, where reciting aloud drew insults from opponents. That closes this plan; thank you for walking from Ar-Ra'd to Al-Isra.
